disclaimer: Each case has three acts: the reason the government gave, with exact quotes and a source; the measure that reason justified, with the official act; and the indicator for the SAME window of time. The page does not claim the measure caused the outcome — it holds the reason to account against whoever asked for the money. Correlation is not causation, and the conclusion is the reader's. Cases not checked in the original document do not appear.
cases[0].justification.paraphrase: Meirelles presented the increase as what preserved fiscal responsibility and balance, and blamed falling revenue: R$ 10.4 billion to meet the primary deficit target of R$ 139 billion.

cases[0].measure.legalNote: The summary of the decree that RAISED the tax says it amends the decrees "that reduce the rates". On paper, the instrument of the increase is an amendment to the decrees of the cut.

cases[0].outcome.steps[0].text: The decree raises PIS/Cofins on fuel to collect R$ 10.4bn and meet the primary deficit target of R$ 139bn.
cases[0].outcome.steps[1].text: The government announces the target is going from R$ 139bn to R$ 159bn, for 2017 and 2018.
cases[0].outcome.steps[2].text: Law 13,480/2017 is signed and the R$ 159bn target becomes law.
cases[0].outcome.steps[3].text: The year closes with a primary deficit of R$ 124.401bn — R$ 34.6bn BELOW the revised R$ 159bn target, and below the R$ 139bn that prompted the increase too.
cases[0].question: If the target could be changed by law in September, why did drivers pay double the PIS/Cofins on petrol from July?
cases[1].justification.paraphrase: Law 14,790/2023 regulated and taxed fixed-odds betting with proceeds earmarked in the statute: of the 12% set aside from revenue, 36% goes to sport, 13.60% to public security and 10% to education. The public argument was that regulating would protect the bettor and bring revenue to those areas.
cases[1].justification.speaker: Federal government
cases[1].justification.role: the bill's rationale and the signing of Law 14,790/2023
cases[1].measure.name: Regulating and taxing fixed-odds betting
cases[1].measure.source: Planalto — the text of the law
cases[1].outcome.indicator: Where the Bolsa Família money went in August 2024
cases[1].outcome.headlineLabel: left Bolsa Família families for betting houses in a single month — and the Central Bank itself says the figure may be understated
cases[1].question: The state legalised it, taxed it and earmarked the revenue for education, sport and security. The following year, four million heads of household on Bolsa Família sent R$ 2 billion to the sector the state had just legalised. Who won the regulation?

cases[1].measure.legalNote: The law earmarks 12% of the revenue, and splits that 12% like this: 36% to sport, 13.60% to public security and 10% to education, among other destinations. That is the promise the regulation carried.
cases[1].outcome.headline: R$ 3 billion
cases[1].outcome.steps[0].text: "It is estimated that, in August 2024, 5 million people belonging to Bolsa Família beneficiary families sent R$ 3 billion to betting companies using Pix, with a MEDIAN of R$ 100 spent per person."
cases[1].outcome.steps[0].source: Central Bank — Special Study 119/2024, requested by senator Omar Aziz
cases[1].outcome.steps[1].text: Of those, 4 million (70%) are heads of household — the people who actually receive the benefit — and on their own they sent R$ 2 billion, two thirds of the total.
cases[1].outcome.steps[2].text: The study itself warns the figure "may be understated": it counted Pix only, leaving credit cards and bank transfers out.
cases[1].outcome.steps[3].text: The betting market moved R$ 20.8 billion a month, against R$ 1.9 billion for the state lottery. Eleven times what the state takes from its own lottery.
cases[1].outcome.steps[3].source: Central Bank — Special Study 119/2024, comparative table
cases[2].justification.paraphrase: The Finance Ministry explained that it raised the IOF temporarily because the Fiscal Responsibility Law requires naming a revenue source for every new mandatory expense — here, the R$ 1.62 billion that Auxílio Brasil would add to continuing mandatory spending still in 2021.
cases[2].justification.speaker: Ministry of the Economy
cases[2].justification.role: in a note released with the decree
cases[2].justification.source: Agência Brasil — publication of the decree raising the IOF
cases[2].measure.name: IOF increase on credit operations to fund Auxílio Brasil
cases[2].measure.legalNote: The decree that RAISED the tax says the rates "are reduced". It is not a mistake: the statute sets higher rates and the decree cuts them, so raising means cutting less. Decree 6,306/2007 set 0.0041% a day for companies and 0.0082% for individuals — the new rates are 36.3% higher. It is the same instrument used for the 2017 PIS/Cofins increase. It ran from 20 September to 31 December 2021 — 103 days.
cases[2].outcome.indicator: The year the tax went up
cases[2].outcome.headlineLabel: is how much the new expense represented of that same year's revenue — and the government raised a tax to cover it
cases[2].outcome.steps[0].text: The decree raises the IOF on credit for 103 days. The Finance Ministry's note acknowledges, in the same sentence, that revenue is at a record level.
cases[2].outcome.steps[1].text: The new expense that needed a source was R$ 1.62 billion in 2021 — what Auxílio Brasil added to continuing mandatory spending.
cases[2].outcome.steps[1].source: Agência Brasil / Ministry of the Economy
cases[2].outcome.steps[2].text: The year closes with R$ 1.879 trillion collected, a record for the series, growing 17.36% above inflation. The R$ 1.62 billion was 0.09% of that.
cases[2].question: Revenue grew 17.36% above inflation and hit a record that same year. If R$ 1.62 billion was missing — nine hundredths of one per cent of what came in — why did the bill go to whoever took out credit?
